item.title: SPECTER Attack Uses USB Power Signals to Leak Data From Air-Gapped PCs
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have demonstrated a covert channel that could allow malware to extract sensitive information from air-gapped computers by manipulating USB power-management settings and observing the resulting signals.

Called SPECTER, the technique was developed by Hyeongjun Choi, Ji Hyuk Jung, and Ji Won Yoon of Korea University in Seoul, South Korea. Their research explores how routine USB control operations can transmit information even when conventional network connections are unavailable.

Turning USB Control Operations Into Signals

Air-gapped systems are physically isolated from external networks to reduce the risk of unauthorized data transfers. However, if an attacker compromises a machine, alternative communication paths may still be available.

SPECTER requires malware to have root or administrator privileges on the compromised host. It encodes information through USB power-management or device-state operations without placing the payload in USB data transfers. The technique involves modifications to peripheral hardware or firmware.

Three Ways to Recover Data

The researchers tested SPECTER on Windows 10 and Ubuntu 22.04, demonstrating three alternative ways to recover the signals.

One method uses smartphone charging states. Researchers used an Android app to read battery-status updates from a Samsung Galaxy S22 running Android 14. On an iPhone 13 Pro running iOS 17.4.1, they watched the on-screen charging indicator instead. The reported signaling rates were 0.2 bits per second on Ubuntu and 0.25 bits per second on Windows for both phones.

They also tested whether changes in USB peripherals could carry the signal. On a Windows laptop, a mouse stopped responding and its LED turned off when disabled, supporting signaling at 1 bit per second. A webcam and USB hub also produced usable signals at 0.25 bits per second.

Researchers did not obtain usable channels with the tested keyboard or headset dongle configurations. None of the tested peripherals produced a usable channel on the Ubuntu desktop, showing that results depend on the host and hardware configuration.

The third method detects near-field electromagnetic activity associated with USB control operations. Using a HackRF One software-defined radio and an LF-R 400 loop antenna in direct contact with the USB cable, the researchers captured signals near 5 MHz. The experiments did not establish reliable reception at a distance.

Low Speeds Limit the Threat

At these rates, SPECTER is unsuitable for transferring large amounts of data. Its potential use lies in extracting short, valuable secrets, such as credentials, authentication tokens or cryptographic keys. However, the experiments do not establish a general error rate or reliable reception at a distance for the RF method.

The findings also highlight limitations to the technique’s stealth. USB control operations can trigger charging notifications, screen activity or interruptions to connected peripherals, depending on the configuration.

Researchers recommend treating USB power-management and device-state events as security-relevant telemetry. Monitoring repeated device enable, disable, suspend and resume operations could help identify suspicious activity, although the effectiveness of such detection remains to be evaluated.

The full research paper is available on arXiv.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: StealC Malware Returns as Stadia RAT After Operation Endgame Takedown
item.description:
StealC’s seller has returned with Stadia RAT, combining credential theft, hidden desktop control, and remote command execution using code reused from StealC v3.5.

Four months after Europol disrupted StealC during Operation Endgame, its seller has returned with Stadia, a new remote access trojan (RAT) that combines credential theft with remote control of Windows systems.

Hackread.com previously reported on StealC’s use in a FileFix phishing campaign in 2025. New research from cybersecurity firm Varonis shared with Hackread.com shows that Stadia reuses code from StealC v3.5 while adding capabilities beyond information theft.

In June 2026, Operation Endgame disrupted StealC and other malware networks. The operation involved 326 servers and 142 domains, while authorities recovered more than 25 million stolen credentials from 385,000 infected machines.

Stadia RAT Expands Beyond Credential Theft

Advertised on October 16, Stadia offers six modules: a stealer, hidden virtual network computing (HVNC), Remote CMD, a loader, File Explorer and Process Manager. These modules let operators steal credentials, control a hidden desktop, execute commands, transfer files, manage processes and load additional payloads.

The stealer targets more than 50 browsers, 120 cryptocurrency browser extensions and 50 desktop wallets, alongside messaging and gaming applications. Subscriptions cost $300/month for Basic, $550/month for Team, and $900/month for Pro, which includes all six modules. Former StealC customers are being offered a free month on the Pro tier.

Code Reuse and Detection

Varonis Threat Labs obtained a 560,128-byte, 32-bit Windows executable and reverse-engineered it to examine how Stadia works. One finding stood out: researchers located a 26,112-byte Chromium App-Bound Encryption helper inside the sample that was identical, byte for byte, to a component found in StealC v3.5. The match provides concrete evidence that the new RAT reuses code from its predecessor.

The sample also checks the system language before proceeding, exiting on machines configured for Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Kazakh or Uzbek, and installing itself on other systems in a randomly named directory under C:\ProgramData\. Here it uses filenames resembling legitimate Windows or software update processes like MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe and SearchHost.exe.

It then creates a hidden scheduled task that runs at logon and every 15 minutes. If it has elevated privileges, Stadia also uses PowerShell to add its installation directory to Microsoft Defender’s exclusion list.

Its network traffic offers another potential detection clue. Stadia sends HTTP POST requests containing RC4-encrypted data encoded in Base64, even though the requests identify their content as application/json.

In its detailed report, Varonis advises defenders to look beyond IP addresses, which can change between builds, and watch for suspicious behavior on infected machines, including unsigned processes injecting code into suspended browser processes, newly created hidden scheduled tasks and unexpected Microsoft Defender exclusions.

Stadia’s return shows the limits of infrastructure takedowns when the people behind a malware operation retain their code and customer base. By adding remote-control tools to StealC’s credential-stealing capabilities and offering former customers a free month, the seller is attempting to rebuild the business with a broader toolkit.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Security Teams and AI Tools: Why Executives Won’t Adopt What They Can’t Control
item.description:
AI is a hot topic for every business. You can’t avoid it, whether CEOs are discussing how to use it to improve productivity or the general public is turning to AI to get quick answers to everyday questions.

For businesses, the appeal is obvious. AI-powered tools can save time, automate repetitive tasks, and make everything from meetings to content creation more efficient – a quick scroll through Instagram and you’ll see a plethora of restaurants using it to advertise their menus, for example. 

But as more businesses introduce AI into their everyday workflows, another question is becoming increasingly important: can people actually use these tools safely?

In the news, there have been a lot of reports on AI safety recently. As you can imagine, there are going to be AI tool adoption barriers, which is why we look into why executives won’t adopt what they can’t control when it comes to AI. 

Visibility is the first challenge

One of the biggest concerns for executives is knowing exactly how AI is being used across an organisation.

Employees may already be using consumer AI platforms to summarise documents, write emails, analyse data or troubleshoot technical problems (we’ve all heard of ChatGPT). If these tools are being used without the knowledge of IT or security teams, organisations can end up with what is effectively an unmanaged layer of technology.

This creates questions around data: What information is being entered into an AI system? Where is that information stored? Who can access it? And what happens to it afterwards?

Without visibility, security teams cannot properly assess or manage the risks.

Control needs to be built in

For AI adoption to scale, businesses need more than policies telling employees what they can and cannot do. They need technical controls that make safe behaviour easier. This could include restricting which AI tools employees can access, controlling what data can be shared, monitoring AI activity, and establishing clear permissions for AI agents interacting with internal systems.

The same principle applies to AI-powered automation. An AI agent that can send emails, access customer records or update business systems needs clearly defined boundaries. Executives are far more likely to approve these technologies when they can see what the AI is allowed to do – and, importantly, what it is prevented from doing.

Security cannot be an afterthought

Traditional software is generally designed around predictable processes. AI systems can behave differently because their outputs can vary depending on the information and instructions they receive.

That makes governance particularly important. Security teams need to be involved before AI tools are deployed rather than being brought in after a problem occurs. They should help establish acceptable use policies, access controls, auditing processes, and mechanisms for stopping or restricting AI activity when necessary.

This doesn’t mean preventing employees from using AI. In fact, excessive restrictions can encourage people to find their own workarounds. Instead, the goal should be controlled adoption.

Overall, the future of workplace AI won’t simply belong to the companies using the most advanced models. It will belong to those that can make AI powerful and controllable. For executives, that distinction could be the difference between approving an AI pilot and rolling it out across the entire organisation.

Which AI tools are you currently using and why? Will you be trying a new one shortly?

item.title: PhantomTac Attack Tricks Robots Into Dropping or Crushing Objects
item.description:
Researchers demonstrated PhantomTac, an attack using hidden magnetic tags to trick robotic touch sensors and make robots drop objects or damage them with force.

A small magnetic tag attached to an object could fool a robot’s magnetic touch sensors, causing it to drop an item, squeeze it too hard or misjudge physical contact.

The details of this attack, called PhantomTac, are described in a research paper by Binbin Zhang, Yifeng Zhang, Xiaomeng Chen, and Dongyao Chen. The paper was posted on October 19 and accepted for the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS) 2026, scheduled for November 15–19 in The Hague, Netherlands.

How PhantomTac Manipulates Sensor Readings

The technique was tested on commercial tactile sensors and real robotic systems. Magnetic tactile sensors detect pressure by tracking changes in a magnetic field as their sensing layer bends or compresses. They measure normal force, which pushes against a surface, and shear force, which acts along the surface.

PhantomTac exploits a limitation in this approach: a small magnet close to the sensor creates a localized magnetic field that may not be cancelled out. The resulting signal can be mistaken for a change in contact force, misleading the robot’s control system.

The researchers developed passive battery-free magnetic tags around 0.5 millimeters thick, with an area as small as 1.44 square centimeters. These can be concealed beneath barcode or QR-code stickers. An attacker needs brief access to an object or its packaging, along with knowledge of the target sensor model, but does not need access to the robot’s software or control system.

Tests Show Risks to Robotic Handling

Researchers evaluated several PaXini sensor models and a XELA uSPa 46 sensor, but used only PaXini hardware for the robotic demonstrations. For context, PaXini and XELA are manufacturers of robotic touch sensors.

The tested models use magnetic fields to measure contact forces, helping robots judge how firmly they are gripping or pressing against an object. Researchers also fitted a Dofbot-Pi4B robotic arm with a magnetic touch sensor to test whether the tags could make its gripper drop or damage an object.

In grasping tests, the attack succeeded more than 95% of the time when the contact position was within 8 millimeters of the intended tag placement.

When the sensor reports more pressure than the robot is actually applying, the robot can start moving before it has a firm grip and drop the item. If the sensor reports too little pressure, the robot can keep squeezing until it damages the object. The paper also examines how false readings of sideways force could weaken its grip.

PhantomTac makes the Dofbot-Pi4B robotic arm underestimate gripping force, causing its gripper to keep closing and crush the object. Video courtesy of the researchers.

PaXini and XELA are manufacturers of robotic touch sensors. The tested models use magnetic fields to measure contact forces, helping robots judge how firmly they are gripping or pressing against an object. In a separate test, a Unitree G1 humanoid robot registered contact before touching a vase or failed to stop before pushing it over, depending on the false reading.

PhantomTac causes the Unitree G1 robot to underestimate contact force, delaying collision detection and causing the vase to topple. Video courtesy of the researchers.

The findings echo a separate study, GhostTac, which examined how electromagnetic interference could manipulate tactile sensors without physical contact. Both studies highlight the risks of relying on potentially manipulated touch readings.

Researchers suggest checking touch readings against motor current, joint torque and movement to identify inconsistent signals. They did not evaluate this proposed defence experimentally. The paper demonstrates controlled attacks, not incidents involving deployed robots.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.
Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: eMudhra to Exit SSL/TLS Market After 8 CA Keys Found Easily Guessable
item.description:
Indian digital trust company eMudhra plans to leave the global SSL/TLS certificate market after eight of its intermediate certificate authorities were found to have easily guessable private keys.

The issue was reported on October 17, 2026, by a researcher identified as Wayne, who reported it to Mozilla. Mozilla independently recovered the keys, and security researcher Scott Helme later demonstrated the weakness in a public analysis, recovering all eight in less than a second. The keys were generated as small numbers rather than the large, unpredictable values expected for cryptographic security, and were created in April 2025.

“The eight intermediates are six TLS issuing CAs (DV, OV and EV, two generations each) and two code-signing CAs, all created in April 2025. Every one of them was also cross-signed by Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services root in May 2025,” Helme explained in his blog post.

eMudhra has attributed the incident to a flaw in its key-generation process and said it is investigating the root cause. Its global SSL/TLS business accounts for roughly 1% of its revenue. The company cited rising compliance costs and data sovereignty requirements as reasons for its exit, while Chairman V Srinivasan described the public scrutiny as disproportionate to the division’s overall importance.

Browsers Withdraw Trust From Affected Certificates

Mozilla blocked the affected intermediates through OneCRL and subsequently moved to remove trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3, the root certificate that signed them. Google has scheduled the removal from Chrome’s Root Store for October 27. Chrome and Firefox had already blocked the six affected TLS intermediates.

According to Google’s public Certificate Transparency records, no TLS certificates chaining to the six affected website-signing intermediates appeared in the logs before they were blocked. However, approximately 30,800 unexpired certificates chained to the broader root hierarchy as of October 21. These were not necessarily issued using the compromised keys.

eMudhra stated that seven of the eight intermediates had never been used in production, while the remaining one had not issued any end-entity certificates.

Earlier Warning Signs

eMudhra is offering free replacement certificates through partners and has committed to maintaining certificate revocation and status services until its issued certificates expire or are replaced.

The incident also raises questions about earlier certificate-management issues. Mozilla’s public incident record shows that eMudhra published invalid certificate revocation lists (CRLs) in May 2025 for six intermediate authorities.

In its current incident investigation, Mozilla questioned why the earlier investigation did not identify that multiple key pairs had been generated for the affected authorities.

The latest incident also has implications beyond browsers. Java keystores, container images, load balancers and mutual TLS configurations may maintain separate trust stores. Java does not check certificate revocation by default, so unpatched environments may continue accepting forged certificates if they still trust the affected chain.

In an October 22 statement, Java platform provider Azul confirmed that it had released updated Azul Zulu Builds of OpenJDK and Azul Prime versions that block the eight compromised certificates. The updates add the certificates to the Java runtime’s blocklist, without requiring manual changes after installation. Azul also published workaround instructions for environments that cannot be updated immediately.

Security teams should review certificate dependencies beyond browsers, apply relevant vendor updates and migrate critical services to an independent, trusted certificate authority where necessary.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Global Premiere: AI Future Forum 2026 in Dubai (2026)

Dubai, UAE, October 26th, 2026, CyberNewswire

AI Future Forum will take place on December 1–2, 2026, in Dubai, alongside Blockchain Life 2026, an international event focused on Web3, crypto, mining, and AI.

Expect visionary founders, global investors, breakthrough AI projects, robotics, and the technologies that will shape the next decade of the digital economy.

With 15,000+ attendees from 130+ countries and 200+ industry-leading speakers, the AI Future Forum is set to become the world’s premier destination where AI, Web3, and crypto leaders come together to shape what’s next.

Event Program:

A full week of live networking with key players from around the world: 2 days of the forum, hundreds of side events, exclusive meetings, and the Formula 1 Grand Prix Final.

200+ top speakers: leading AI experts, founders of technology companies, investors, representatives of top AI startups, and leaders of the digital industry. The focus will be on the practical application of AI, its integration with crypto and business, and the technologies shaping the new digital economy.

A large-scale expo zone: 200+ leading companies in robotics, AI development, Web3 projects, and the most progressive startups.

The legendary AfterParty at one of Dubai’s top clubs with a globally known headline artist.

Startup Pitch – an opportunity to present your project to the international community and attract attention from investors and funds.

An AI Future Forum ticket includes access to Blockchain Life 2026. A 10% ticket discount is available with promo code CHAINWIRE through the event website.

About AI Future:

AI Future Forum 2026 will take place on December 1–2 in Dubai as part of Blockchain Life Forum. The event brings together entrepreneurs, investors, developers, and startups at the intersection of AI and Web3.

On one platform, crypto investors, funds, and tech teams will explore real-world AI applications, new business models, and opportunities in the digital economy.

Attendees will gain insights from industry leaders, discover practical use cases, and connect through high-level international networking.

The forum takes place just ahead of the Formula 1 Grand Prix Final, bringing together the global tech community in Dubai.

Blockchain Life

item.title: 12,976 Refrigeration Controls Found Exposed Online in 99 Countries
item.description:
Cyberattacks affecting more than 700 supermarkets in France in October 2026 involved manipulated refrigeration temperatures and defrost settings, causing food losses. CERT-FR confirmed compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC systems, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB equipment. As Hackread.com previously reported, the attackers’ identities and precise method of gaining access remain unconfirmed.

Against this backdrop, cybersecurity researchers at Forescout’s Vedere Labs identified 12,976 internet-exposed refrigeration service observations across 6,017 public IP addresses in 99 countries and territories.

The researchers used Shodan, a search engine for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, to identify exposed services across 10 product groups. The figures represent service observations rather than individual refrigeration systems, as one IP address can expose multiple interfaces or represent several downstream systems.

The report warns that exposed management interfaces and software vulnerabilities can let cybercriminals manipulate refrigeration systems. This indicates a serious risk for industries that depend on temperature-controlled storage such as supermarkets, hospitals, agricultural facilities and pharmaceutical supply chains.

Supermarket Attacks Highlight the Risks

Forescout also tracked more than 20 claimed attacks against refrigeration systems since January 2026, with pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) among the most active. Targets included wineries, fruit storage facilities, supermarkets and food-processing sites across Europe.

On April 26 alone, Z-Pentest claimed 10 attacks. The threat predates this year’s incidents. According to a Danfoss technical bulletin published in October 2025, earlier attacks in 2022 affected 16 Russian supermarkets and 40 Israeli stores.

Thousands of Refrigeration Services Exposed Online

Forescout identified the following internet-exposed services, grouped by product family. The company also found that 80% of observed Danfoss StoreView services were running older firmware potentially affected by known vulnerabilities.

The following exposed services were identified:

Forescout also found that 80% of observed Danfoss StoreView services were running older firmware potentially affected by known vulnerabilities.

Danfoss’ August 2025 advisories described two vulnerabilities affecting AK-SM 8xxA systems running versions before 4.3.1. CVE-2025-41451 could allow remote code execution through command injection, while CVE-2025-41452 could cause a denial-of-service condition through web interface configuration changes.

Both require authentication before exploitation but highlight the risks posed by vulnerable refrigeration management equipment.

Hospitals Could Face Similar Refrigeration Risks

The attacks in France show how changing refrigeration settings can cause real-world losses without deploying destructive malware. In hospitals, similar interference could spoil vaccines, medicines and other temperature-sensitive supplies.

Forescout warned that attacks on these systems can have “physical and financial consequences” even when attackers use legitimate control functions rather than destructive malware. Its research does not report confirmed attacks on hospital refrigeration networks, but the number of exposed systems raises questions about how well these devices are protected.

Many refrigeration systems can be accessed remotely for maintenance, sometimes by third-party contractors responsible for several sites. Forescout warned that stolen or shared contractor credentials could put these systems at risk, particularly when their management interfaces are exposed online. An attacker with access could alter temperatures or defrost settings without deploying malware.

Forescout recommends restricting direct internet access, securing remote connections, giving contractors individual accounts with multifactor authentication, patching vulnerable systems and monitoring unusual changes to settings or alarms.

Experts Warn of Risks to Hospitals and Critical Infrastructure

Damon Small, board member at Xcape Inc., shared with Hackread.com his concerns about the potential impact on healthcare facilities.

“Unprotected refrigeration controllers represent an immediate threat to clinical operations and patient safety, where even slight temperature variations can spoil irreplaceable lab specimens, degrade critical pharmaceuticals, and interrupt acute care,” Small said.

He warned that attackers could manipulate refrigeration settings without triggering physical alarms in time, adding that security teams must treat environmental controls as critical operational assets.

“If an industrial chiller is easier to access from the Internet than your patient portal, your security architecture has melted,” Small added.

Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of BreachLock, also shared his perspective with Hackread.com, pointing to recent incidents involving refrigeration and cold-chain operations.

“Nearly 13,000 refrigeration systems reachable from the public internet across 99 countries is the picture underneath incidents the industry has already seen this year,” Sehgal said.

He warned that hospitals should check which refrigeration units are accessible online, whether their software is up to date, and what happens if temperature controls stop responding outside normal working hours.

“A pentest of the refrigeration environment, specifically what an attacker could reach and change from the controllers themselves, is the right way to answer those questions before someone else answers them during an incident,” Sehgal added.

(Photo by Jude Ballado by Pexels)

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Criminal IP Joins INTERPOL’s Gateway Initiative to Support Global Cybercrime Efforts
item.description:
Torrance, United States / California, October 27th, 2026, CyberNewswire

AI SPERA, the company behind the cyber threat intelligence and attack surface management platform Criminal IP, has signed a cooperation agreement with the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL) under its Gateway initiative. The agreement establishes a framework for sharing information and technical expertise relevant to cybercrime analysis.

Established in 2019, INTERPOL’s Gateway initiative provides a secure framework for sharing cyber threat intelligence with trusted private sector partners, including cybersecurity companies, technology providers and financial institutions. Partners can contribute indicators of compromise, insights into cybercriminal tactics and techniques, and threat analysis. INTERPOL reviews this information alongside other intelligence to develop investigative leads, which may be shared with member countries concerned by a threat.

Under the agreement, Criminal IP plans to contribute threat data, analysis and technical expertise to support INTERPOL’s cybercrime efforts. Criminal IP provides intelligence on IP addresses, domains and internet-exposed assets, helping analysts investigate suspicious infrastructure and identify connections between cyber threats. The cooperation aims to apply these capabilities to the development of intelligence relevant to cross-border investigations.

“Our participation in INTERPOL’s Gateway initiative marks a meaningful milestone for Criminal IP,” said Byungtak Kang, CEO of Criminal IP. “Cybercrime crosses borders, and effective investigations depend on timely intelligence and cooperation between the public and private sectors. We look forward to contributing our threat intelligence and technical expertise to this shared effort.”                                                                                                  

About Criminal IP

Criminal IP is a cyber threat intelligence solution operated by AI SPERA that provides decision-ready threat intelligence, and AI-powered threat exposure management solutions to security teams worldwide. By continuously scanning the global internet, Criminal IP aggregates and contextualizes threat signals across IPs, domains, URLs, and attack infrastructure, covering malicious indicators, known vulnerabilities, exposed assets, and attacker behavior.

Criminal IP’s mission is to give organizations real visibility into their cyber landscape and accelerate threat detection and response by delivering the intelligence needed to outsmart attackers. For more information, visit www.criminalip.io

Contact

Michael Sena
AI SPERA
[email protected]

item.title: Hackers Abuse Microsoft Teams External Chats to Access Corporate PCs
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers from Arctic Wolf Labs have uncovered a widespread campaign involving the abuse of Microsoft Teams’ default external chat settings to gain initial access to corporate networks.

Researchers reviewed more than 400 incidents involving this technique and found that this campaign relies on impersonation and social engineering to gain employees’ trust.

In many cases, scammers’ main objective was to gain remote access to their victims’ computers. These findings were shared exclusively with Hackread.com.

How the Attacks Unfold

Microsoft Teams comes with an external access feature enabled by default. It allows users from other Microsoft 365 tenants to contact employees when external access is permitted by both organizations unless the feature is manually restricted.

Attackers exploit this feature by creating temporary tenants. Researchers found that 30% to 40% of analyzed cases involved default .onmicrosoft.com domains, which can be provisioned within minutes without verifying a custom domain.

Attackers impersonate IT staff using names such as “IT Support” and “IT Service Desk.” Some append “(Internal)” to their display names to make external contacts appear legitimate, despite Teams marking them as external. Arctic Wolf also observed more than 100 emoji markers in attacker display names, suggesting possible AI-assisted identity creation, although this has not been confirmed.

In many cases, the Teams contact follows “mail bombing,” which floods victims’ inboxes with hundreds of subscription confirmations within minutes. The disruption creates urgency and can bury legitimate security alerts, making the fake IT support offer more convincing.

From Teams Chat to Network Reconnaissance

After establishing contact, attackers, posing as IT support, try to convince an employee to allow remote access to their computer. They use vishing (voice phishing) through Teams calls and remote monitoring and management (RMM) software like Quick Assist. However, researchers also found cases involving the use of other RMM tools like AnyDesk and TeamViewer.

In one case researchers examined, the employee was tricked into running a PowerShell command that downloaded a malicious MSI installer. The installer placed an obfuscated script in the user’s AppData folder. The script then decoded and ran more malicious code.

The attack also installed a Python-based implant, which queried Active Directory for information about user and computer accounts. It then sent the data to the attackers’ command-and-control (C2) servers, giving them information about the organisation’s network.

What Organizations Can Do

This research shows how quickly a convincing support request can turn into a wider intrusion. “Chat creation itself is only the entry point,” researchers noted in the blog post, adding that for organizations the risk is not simply that an employee answers a suspicious message, but that trusting the wrong person with remote access can let them explore the corporate network.

Researchers recommend limiting external Teams chats to approved partner domains, blocking chats from unmanaged accounts and trial-only tenants, and restricting Quick Assist and unauthorized remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools.

Employees should verify unexpected IT support requests through a trusted channel and remember that a sender using “Internal” in their display name does not prove they are part of the IT team.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Microsoft Issues Emergency .NET Fixes for Brotli Flaw and Linux Privilege Escalation
item.description:
Microsoft has released emergency security updates for .NET 8, .NET 9, .NET 10 and .NET 11 Release Candidate 3 (RC3), fixing a buffer overflow flaw and a Linux vulnerability that could let local attackers gain higher privileges. The company has urged developers and administrators to install the updates as soon as possible.

The October 25 out-of-band release also revisits two vulnerabilities that Microsoft’s October 13 security updates did not fully fix. The latest release addresses both issues again, alongside the newly disclosed flaws. Hackread.com previously reported on Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday, when the company released fixes for a record 1,413 vulnerabilities.

What the Vulnerabilities Could Allow

The most serious issue, CVE-2026-111497, affects Brotli- a compression technology used to reduce the size of data transferred or processed by applications. A flaw in how .NET handles this data could let an attacker read or corrupt a program’s memory without first logging in. Depending on the application and circumstances, this could expose information, crash a service or allow an attacker to gain higher privileges.

The vulnerability affects .NET applications on all platforms, but exposure depends on how they handle compressed data. Microsoft specifically identifies ASP.NET Core request decompression, automatic response decompression in HttpClient, and the Brotli APIs in System.IO.Compression as affected paths. The automatic decompression features are off by default, and .NET Framework is not affected.

The same Brotli decoder flaw also affects other software, including Node.js. On October 26, Tenable reported that proof-of-concept code was publicly available and that researchers had demonstrated remote code execution in Node.js. It also reported an attempted exploitation targeting Node.js, but noted that it had not independently confirmed the activity.

A second flaw, CVE-2026-114148, affects Linux .NET tarballs containing unsafe file ownership information. A local attacker could use this issue to change files and gain elevated privileges. It affects source-build tarballs for .NET 10 and .NET 11. On .NET 8 and .NET 9, affected ASP.NET Core tarball distributions are also included, even when users do not build .NET from source.

Updates and Deployment Requirements

Microsoft has also reissued fixes for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw involving SocketAsyncEventArgs, and CVE-2026-102870, which affects the Blazor WebAssembly debugger. The October 13 updates did not fully address either issue.

The updated releases are .NET 8.0.33, 9.0.22 and 10.0.14, alongside .NET 11 RC3. Users running .NET 11 RC2 should upgrade to RC3.

How the updates are applied depends on the deployment because applications using a shared .NET runtime need the updated runtime installed and must be restarted, while applications bundled with their own runtime must be rebuilt and republished. Container deployments require new images and redeployment.

Those building .NET from source must rebuild their packages using updated artifacts. Users of affected ASP.NET Core tarballs on .NET 8 and .NET 9 must install the refreshed versions. Updating the host system alone will not patch a runtime bundled inside an application or container.

Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of BreachLock, highlighted the potential consequences if attackers exploit the Brotli flaw in a vulnerable .NET process.

“When vulnerabilities like CVE-2026-111497 are left unpatched, an attacker exploiting this chain can start with memory corruption inside a vulnerable .NET process, escalate privileges against the service account running it, and inherit whatever reach that account has. Enterprises typically grant those accounts more reach than they need,” Sehgal told Hackread.com.

He urged organizations to identify the runtime versions running in production and establish who is responsible for each deployment.

“Teams that already know what runtime versions are running in production and who owns each one will patch this fast. The rest should start that inventory work now,” he said.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.
